title: A Scoping Review of Occupational Risk Assessment Methods: Classification, Advantages, Limitations and Application Areas
content:
Background: Occupational risk assessment is a mandatory procedure in modern occupational health and safety (OHS) management systems worldwide. However, no single regulatory document prescribes the use of a specific assessment method, leaving organizations with a wide choice of available tools. The diversity of existing approaches – from simple checklists to complex probabilistic models – creates a methodological challenge for practitioners and researchers, particularly in high-risk industries such as coal mining.

Objectives: This scoping review aims to systematically map and classify existing occupational risk assessment methods, identify their key advantages and limitations and determine their typical application areas. The review also examines the regulatory requirements for risk assessment in Russian and international practice.

Eligibility Criteria: The review included methods and approaches for occupational risk assessment published in peer-reviewed journals, regulatory documents and industry guidelines in English or Russian, supplemented by Persian-language sources indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, which were fully translated into English for de-tailed methodological review, over the past 30 years. Methods were included if they provided a structured approach to hazard identification, risk estimation or risk evaluation applicable to occupational settings.

Sources of Evidence: A systematic search was conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar and Russian scientific databases (eLIBRARY.ru) using keywords related to occupational risk assessment, hazard identification and risk analysis methods.

Charting Methods: Data were extracted using a standardized form and grouped by methodological principle into eleven thematic blocks. Each method was described in terms of its core principle, advantages, limitations and typical application areas.

Results: Fifty-five distinct methods were identified and classified into eleven blocks: (1) qualitative hazard identification; (2) engineering reliability analysis; (3) scenario modeling and barrier analysis; (4) human reliability assessment; (5) semi-quantitative ranking methods; (6) probabilistic and statistical methods; (7) uncertainty and multi-criteria hybrids; (8) hygienic and health risk assessment; (9) ergonomic and biomechanical risks; (10) psychosocial risks; (11) behavioral safety and strategic management. A comparative analysis revealed that no single method is universally applicable; the choice depends on data availability, assessment objectives and organizational con-text.

Conclusions: This scoping review provides a comprehensive map of existing occupational risk assessment methods, offering researchers and practitioners a structured framework for selecting appropriate tools based on their specific needs. The classification highlights the complementary nature of different approaches and the necessity of hybrid methodologies for complex industrial settings.
